query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partial substitution of heavier refractory elements with aluminum in a Ti-Nb-Ta-V-based high-entropy alloy increases high-temperature yield strength and reduces density while preserving room-temperature ductility and strength by promoting a B2-precipitation-mediated strengthening mechanism.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline Ti-Nb-Ta-V refractory high-entropy alloy without aluminum content, produced by vacuum arc melting and homogenized.
generation.intervention: Introduce 5-10 at.% Al in place of heavier refractory elements (e.g., Ta or Nb) during alloy melting.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests under uniaxial compression or tension from room temperature up to ≥1200 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of B2-ordered precipitates in a predominantly BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Al additions reduce overall density and promote the B2 phase, refining microstructure and impeding dislocation motion, leading to enhanced high-temperature strength while maintaining room-temperature ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: A 10–20% increase in compressive or tensile yield strength relative to the Al-free baseline at 1200 °C, with no more than a minor (≤5%) reduction in room-temperature strength.
generation.baseline: Ti-Nb-Ta-V alloy (Al-free) tested under identical mechanical loading conditions.
generation.boundary: Performance gains may diminish or invert if Al additions exceed ~10 at.%, causing excessive brittle intermetallic formation or if the alloy is exposed to prolonged thermal cycling that destabilizes B2 precipitates.
generation.uncertainty: Long-term creep performance and oxidation resistance at ultra-high temperatures are not yet fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two alloy variants: the baseline (Al-free) and the same alloy with 5–10 at.% Al. Cast and homogenize both similarly, then machine samples for mechanical testing at elevated temperatures (e.g., 1000–1200 °C). Also measure density and room-temperature tensile properties.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and ductility at room temperature
Tensile or compressive yield strength at 1000–1200 °C
Microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM, EBSD, TEM) of precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-modified alloy does not exhibit a measurable improvement (≥10%) in high-temperature strength relative to the baseline, or if its room-temperature ductility drops significantly (e.g., >10% reduction), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractA series of TaNbVTiAlx (x = 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0) refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) with high specific strength and reasonable plasticity were prepared using powder metallurgy (P/M) technology. This paper studied their microstructure and compression properties. The results show that all the TaNbVTiAlx RHEAs exhibited a single BCC solid solution microstructure with no elemental segregation. The P/M TaNbVTiAlx RHEAs showed excellent room-temperature specific strength (207.11 MPa*cm3/g) and high-temperature specific strength (88.37 MPa*cm3/g at 900 °C and 16.03 MPa*cm3/g at 1200 °C), with reasonable plasticity, suggesting that these RHEAs have potential to be applied at temperatures >1200 °C. Besides PBF-LB/M, different additive manufacturing processes such as wire arc additive manufacturing [], electron beam melting [,] or laser liquid phase sintering [] of 3d transition metal high entropy alloys are subjects of ongoing research. In contrast to that, refractory metal high entropy alloys are by far less investigated []. First results on the alloys WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV were reported by Senkov et al., in 2010 [] and 2011 [], respectively. Refractory metal high entropy alloys possess a wide range of material properties depending on the alloy compositions and are especially interesting for high temperature applications []. Since the first publications different refractory metal high entropy alloy compositions and alloy design approaches were investigated with the aim to increase e.g., room temperature ductility [] or to decrease the density of the alloys by replacing heavy elements like Ta and W by lighter elements. Senkov et al. reported a beneficial effect of an Al addition on the mechanical properties of MoNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr refractory metal high entropy alloys [], while also reducing the density of the alloy. Yet, RHEAs are also able to exhibit superalloy-like microstructures [,,,], often possessing coherent BCC_A2 and BCC_B2 phase relationships similar to those FCC_A1 and FCC_L12 structures exhibited by Ni-based superalloys []. These are responsible for the excellent high-temperature stability and properties of these alloys. The main challenge in dealing with refractory alloys is that they are often brittle [,,], especially at room temperature. However, under certain processing conditions, these novel RHEAs possess a high strength combined with a satisfactory ductility level at both room and high temperatures [,,,], performing superiorly compared to some of the commercial Ni-based superalloys []. In particular, the Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr composition and its variants have stood out as potential alternatives for the production of strong and ductile refractory high-entropy superalloys [,,]. HEAs are widely produced by liquid state methods, such as casting by vacuum arc-melting, induction melting, etc. [,].
